# Machine Payments Protocol interop harness

The wire encodings in `packages/core/src/mpp` exist to agree with somebody
else, so they are checked against somebody else. The other implementation is
the Go `mpp` package in
[aperture](https://github.com/lightninglabs/aperture), and this directory
holds the tooling that checks both directions of that agreement.

## Go to TypeScript: `vectors.json`

`vectors.json` is generated by aperture's `mpp/mppvectors` package and copied
here verbatim. **Do not edit it.** A hand-edited vector proves agreement with
nobody: the file's whole value is that it records what the peer actually does,
including the parts we would not have thought to check.

Regenerate it from an aperture checkout:

```sh
cd /path/to/aperture
go run ./cmd/gen-mpp-vectors -o - > /path/to/aperture-ts/packages/core/testdata/mpp/vectors.json
pnpm --filter @aperture/core test
```

Aperture's own `TestVectorsAreCurrent` fails if its committed copy has drifted
from what the generator produces, so the file there is always current with the
Go code. Copying it here is the only step that can go stale, and the tests
below are what catch it.

The `version` field is the schema version. `goVectors.ts` refuses a file whose
version it does not recognize, rather than looping over undefined fields and
passing over nothing.

Every group in the file is consumed:

| group              | checked by            |
| ------------------ | --------------------- |
| `canonicalization` | `jcs.test.ts`         |
| `base64url`        | `base64url.test.ts`   |
| `challengeIds`     | `challengeId.test.ts` |
| `challengeHeaders` | `header.test.ts`      |
| `challengeLists`   | `header.test.ts`      |
| `credentials`      | `header.test.ts`      |
| `receipts`         | `header.test.ts`      |

## TypeScript to Go: the transcript

Vectors prove that TypeScript reproduces Go's bytes. They cannot prove that
Go accepts TypeScript's, which is the direction a buyer actually depends on.
`emit_transcript.mjs` produces a buyer transcript, and
`verify_transcript.go` replays it as the seller: it parses each
`WWW-Authenticate` header, verifies the challenge id binds to the parsed
parameters, parses the `Authorization` credential, and recomputes the HMAC
from the echoed challenge, which is exactly what an aperture handler does.

```sh
pnpm -r build
cd packages/core/testdata/mpp && node emit_transcript.mjs > /tmp/transcript.json

# From a scratch module with the aperture checkout wired in, and
# verify_transcript.go copied alongside.
go run verify_transcript.go /tmp/transcript.json
```

## TypeScript to Go: the session state machine

The codec transcript cannot catch a buyer that encodes everything perfectly
and still speaks the wrong protocol, which is exactly the failure that
strands a deposit: the server creates a session only from an `open`
credential carrying the deposit preimage and the return invoice, demands the
preimage on every bearer request, and credits a top-up only from a `topUp`
credential proving the fresh invoice's preimage.

`emit_session_transcript.mjs` runs a real `createPayingFetch` lifecycle
(open, bearer, top-up, bearer, close) against a scripted seller and records
every credential it produced. `verify_session_transcript.go` replays them
through `auth.MPPSessionAuthenticator`, the reference component that makes
those decisions, and also checks the transitions around replays: a bearer
before its open is refused, a replayed open is refused, a replayed topUp is
accepted without crediting twice, and a close only works once.

```sh
pnpm -r build
cd packages/core/testdata/mpp
node emit_session_transcript.mjs > /tmp/session_transcript.json

# The scratch module needs aperture's own requires and replaces, since the
# authenticator pulls in lnd and btcd: seed go.mod from aperture's, rename
# the module, add a require and a local replace for
# github.com/lightninglabs/aperture, copy its go.sum, and drop
# verify_session_transcript.go alongside (with the ignore tag removed, or
# named explicitly on the go run command line).
go run verify_session_transcript.go /tmp/session_transcript.json
```

The return invoice in the emit script is a real amountless regtest BOLT11
invoice with a ten-year expiry, because the authenticator zpay32-decodes it
and refuses an open whose refund path it cannot parse.

## Where the two implementations still differ

One difference is left, and it is deliberate rather than pending.

**Credential JSON.** The Go canonicalizer follows RFC 8785 and leaves `<`,
`>`, `&`, U+2028 and U+2029 literal, but its credential encoder is a plain
`json.Marshal`, which escapes the first three for HTML safety. So a credential
echoing a description like `Q&A endpoint` goes out as different bytes from
each side, and each side reads the other's back to the same document.

This side does not follow. Nothing signs a credential: a seller recomputes the
challenge HMAC from the decoded parameters, and `description` is not one of the
seven slots that HMAC covers. `request` and `opaque` are base64url and cannot
contain any of the five characters. Adding HTML escaping back to one encoder to
match a peer that is escaping by accident would reintroduce, one function over,
exactly the divergence that was taken out of the canonicalizer. The divergence
is pinned by a test in `header.test.ts` so that it stays a decision rather than
a surprise.
